Issued at 1208 PM CST Wed Nov 18 2026

The forecast over the next week features several moving pieces, 
though no major hazardous weather conditions are expected locally. 
Early Wednesday afternoon day-cloud phase satellite captures stratus 
over much of MN, located within a southerly warm advective regime 
east of deepening surface cyclone over central ND. The surface low 
is associated with a negatively tilted trough that is set to pivot 
over the Plains through the rest of the day, which supports further 
deepening of the surface low. In the lower levels, a 40-50kt LLJ 
currently extends from eastern NE - central IA - into SE MN. Surface 
winds have increased in response to the deepening cyclone and 
orientation of the LLJ, which has yielded sustained flow of 15-25 
mph and observed gusts between 30-40 mph (the strongest across 
southwestern portions of MN). We are seeing some erosion of the 
stratus across far western MN and into portions of northwest IA, so 
there is some optimism that we'll have at least some filtered 
sunshine over more of the forecast area this afternoon. However, 
forecast soundings along and north of I-94 remain pessimistic with 
the degree of clearing until after sunset. Despite the stratus, 
should continue to see temperatures climb well into the 50s within 
the warm advection regime. The warmest temperatures are expected 
along the Buffalo Ridge, where temperatures are forecast to warm 
into the lower 60s. Southerly winds will diminish slightly heading 
into this evening, though 20-30 mph gusts are still expected. 

Surface low pressure will pivot north into southern Canada tonight 
and translate eastward across Ontario tomorrow. This evolution will 
send a cold front eastward across the forecast area, resulting in a 
westerly shift in the winds for Thursday. Westerly gusts between 25-
35 mph are expected, with the strongest winds along and north of I-
94 as this portion of the area is closest to the departing synoptic 
low. As has been the trend, we anticipate a dry frontal passage and 
any wrap-around showers should remain well to the north tomorrow. 
Departing cloud cover will set the stage for another mild afternoon 
with mostly sunny skies and highs in the 50s. Calm conditions return 
Thursday evening into Friday morning.

By early Friday, forecast guidance displays the next trough in the 
series approaching the Four Corner region, with a quick translation 
across the Plains forecast to occur through early Saturday. 
Associated surface low pressure is progged to develop across the 
central Plains and lift northeast through roughly Fargo/Grand Forks. 
Given this track, our forecast area will remain on the warm side of 
the system -- in fact, the preceding wing of warm advection looks to 
be impressive (+10-12C 850 mb temp anomaly) which will yield surface 
highs in the mid 60s across much of the area Friday afternoon. This 
time around, the upper-level trough remains positively tilted, so we 
see a bit of a slower evolution and translation of the surface 
features. Essentially, this means we'll hang onto the mild air to 
open Saturday morning (mid 50s across eastern MN/western WI at 7 
AM!), prior to the eastward passage of a cold front. The slower 
progression will likely result in a bit of a temperature gradient 
through Saturday, with locations across western MN stuck in the 40s 
for the duration, while locations in western WI hang onto the upper 
50s (perhaps another 60) through the afternoon.

As far as precipitation chances go, we're carrying a slight chance 
for showers along and north of the warm front (central MN) Friday 
evening, but the higher chances will be associated with the cold 
frontal passage on Saturday. The overall trend has been for 
precipitation potential to be more confined to far eastern MN and 
western WI, with several scenarios depicting a sharp cut-off in QPF 
from east to west across the TC Metro. However, there are multiple 
global ensemble members that display QPF west of the Metro, which is 
why chance PoPs (30-50 percent) exist as far west as they do in the 
latest NBM run. As more of the hi-res data mixes into the blend (and 
if the eastward trend continues), we should see the PoP forecast 
tighten up a bit. The latest QPF forecast illustrates this idea, 
with potential for 0.25-0.5" along and east of a line from Faribault 
to Barron counties. Consensus solution places the heaviest axis of 
QPF (amounts near 1") southeast of the forecast area into WFO ARX's 
CWA. 

Much colder air flows into the Upper Midwest Saturday night into
